results.title: Nebius Introduces Dynamic Spot Pricing for GPU VMs as AI Compute Demand Tightens | AI Industry Today
highlights:
Nebius is turning unused GPU capacity into a real-time compute market. From October 8, preemptible VM prices will adjust by GPU type and region as often as every 15 minutes based on available supply and customer demand, with users able either to cap the price they are willing to pay or follow the market to maximize availability. Coming just after Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates amid strong AI demand, the move shows neocloud pricing splitting into premium guaranteed capacity and dynamically priced interruptible compute — making when and where an AI workload runs an increasingly important part of compute economics.

...

Nebius is introducing dynamic spot pricing for its preemptible virtual machines, replacing fixed discounts with market-based GPU prices that respond to real-time capacity and customer demand. Nebius said the new pricing system will take effect on October 8 and will calculate a separate spot price for each GPU type and region, giving AI developers more flexibility to trade off compute availability against cost.

Until now, Nebius priced preemptible VMs by applying discounts set by the company to its standard on-demand rates. Under the new system, an algorithm will aggregate available capacity and demand signals from Nebius customers and update the spot price as frequently as every 15 minutes. Prices will remain between a predefined floor and ceiling, with the ceiling set one cent below the corresponding on-demand GPU-hour rate.

Customers will be able to choose between two pricing strategies. Users focused on minimizing cost can set a maximum price per GPU-hour for a specific accelerator and region. If the spot price is at or below that threshold, the workload runs at the prevailing market price. If the price rises above the user’s limit, the preemptible instance stops while its data is retained and can be restarted once pricing falls back within the specified range.

...

In ... Kubernetes can automatically restart interrupted preemptible instances, while standalone VMs can be restarted manually or through Terraform, SDKs, APIs or command-line tools.

...

The change comes as AI compute remains unusually tight. Reuters reported last week that Nebius will raise on-demand prices for selected Nvidia GPUs by 17% to 21% from October 1, its second increase in three months. The company cited surging demand for infrastructure used to train and run AI models, while also raising prices on some CPU and memory resources.

Current Nebius pricing shows how large the gap between interruptible and guaranteed capacity can be. Before the dynamic system takes effect, Nebius lists preemptible B200 capacity at $3.95 per GPU-hour versus $7.15 on demand, H200 at $2.45 versus $4.50, and H100 at $2.15 versus $3.85. Those fixed preemptible rates will be replaced by the new demand-sensitive mechanism from October 8.

The shift effectively creates a more explicit market for unused AI compute inside Nebius’ cloud. When GPU supply is abundant relative to short-term demand, customers with flexible workloads may be able to access capacity at lower prices; when demand tightens, spot prices can rise toward the on-demand rate. The result moves AI infrastructure pricing closer to the model already familiar in power markets and traditional cloud computing, where interruptible capacity is priced dynamically to balance utilization and demand.

results.title: Nvidia B200 Rental Prices Surge Toward $8 per GPU-Hour as Blackwell Compute Tightens | AI Industry Today
highlights:
Nvidia B200 rental compute is becoming more expensive again. The transaction-based Ornn index has risen to $7.77 per GPU-hour — up 17.1% in a month and the highest level in its public three-month window — while dedicated GPU clouds show a current median of $7.88. Different trackers report different absolute prices because they measure different provider and transaction sets, but the direction is consistent: flexible Blackwell capacity remains tight enough that B200 rental prices are rising even as newer accelerators begin entering the market.

...

Nvidia B200 rental prices have climbed toward $8 per GPU-hour as demand for Blackwell compute continues to put pressure on available cloud capacity. The transaction-based Ornn Compute Price Index for the B200 settled at $7.77 per GPU-hour on September 22, up 7.8% over seven days and 17.1% over the past month. The reading is the highest level in Ornn’s publicly available three-month history.

A separate measure of publicly listed on-demand pricing shows a similar level. GetDeploying’s latest weekly dataset puts the median B200 price across dedicated GPU clouds at $7.88 per GPU-hour, while major hyperscalers charge a median of $15.26. The $7.88 figure is therefore a provider median rather than a single transaction price or universal market average.

The distinction matters because GPU rental markets remain fragmented. Ornn calculates its benchmark from executed neocloud transactions using a volume-weighted methodology, while public-price trackers generally compare provider rate cards. Price of Compute, for example, showed a live on-demand median of $6.79 across five providers on September 23, with individual prices ranging from $5.43 at Massed Compute to $8.60 at CoreWeave.

Despite the differences in methodology, the datasets point in the same direction: premium Blackwell capacity remains expensive and recent transaction prices are rising. Ornn’s B200 benchmark has climbed from $6.64 per GPU-hour a month ago to $7.77, while its H200 index currently sits at $4.94 and H100 at $2.85. On a raw GPU-hour basis, the B200 therefore rents for about 57% more than an H200 and roughly 2.7 times the price of an H100.

That premium does not directly mean the B200 is more expensive per unit of useful AI work. Blackwell provides substantially higher throughput and memory capacity than Hopper-generation accelerators, so training or inference workloads that make full use of the architecture can finish with fewer GPU-hours. The rising rental rate instead shows how much customers are currently willing to pay for access to the newest high-end Nvidia compute.

Availability remains an important part of the pricing picture. Compute.world currently classifies B200 capacity as “booked / sales-gated,” citing constrained near-term availability at several major providers. Lambda’s public on-demand rate is around $6.69 per GPU-hour for an eight-GPU B200 configuration, while CoreWeave is listed at $8.60. Some cheaper listings exist, but immediate availability varies significantly by provider and region.

Nvidia itself continues to acknowledge supply constraints across its latest data center systems. In its latest quarterly filing, Nvidia said Blackwell represented the majority of its system shipments and that the company was experiencing certain supply constraints as it simultaneously ramps Blackwell and next-generation Vera Rubin products. Nvidia has entered into large manufacturing and supply commitments to secure capacity for the coming years.

At the current Ornn settlement, continuously renting one B200 would cost roughly $5,597 over a 30-day, 720-hour month. An eight-GPU deployment at the same benchmark would imply nearly $44,800 per month before accounting for differences in CPU, networking, storage or managed-service configurations. The economics help explain why large AI developers increasingly seek long-term capacity contracts or build dedicated infrastructure rather than relying entirely on burst on-demand compute.

The rise in B200 pricing is also notable because the normal lifecycle of compute hardware tends to push rental prices lower as supply expands and newer accelerators arrive. The current move in the opposite direction suggests that incremental AI demand is absorbing new Blackwell capacity faster than additional supply is reaching the flexible rental market, at least in the neocloud segment captured by the transaction index.

Whether the price remains near current highs will depend on several competing forces. Continued expansion of frontier-model training and inference would support demand, while wider deployments of B300 and Vera Rubin systems could eventually free B200 capacity and pressure rental rates. For now, however, the latest market data suggests that access to high-end Blackwell compute remains a scarce resource rather than a rapidly depreciating commodity.

results.title: Spot GPU discounts run from 81.5% to nothing, September 2026
highlights:
On 2026-09-23 the discount on a spot GPU-hour runs from 81.5% at one provider down to nothing at another. Across the 42 spot rates we can set against the same provider’s own on-demand rate for the same card, the typical discount is 50%. The deepest belongs to Microsoft Azure’s H100 SXM in eastus; the shallowest are at Nebius, which since 2026-09-22 lists two of its cards at the same figure in both columns.

That last part is new. At 14:38 UTC on 2026-09-22 Nebius rewrote both columns of its price list in one go. Its H100 SXM spot rate went from $2.15 to $3.85 per GPU-hour, a rise of 79.1%; its L40S spot rate went from $0.74 to $1.55, a rise of 109.5%. Four on-demand rates moved in the same read, by 16.9% to 21.0%. The rate card at nebius.com/prices prints those figures.

...

A spot rate is capacity the provider can reclaim, and the discount is what it pays a renter for accepting that. On 2026-09-23 the payment is not one number. For the H100 SXM alone we read 81.5% below on-demand at Microsoft Azure, 60.4% at CoreWeave in Europe, 50% at DataCrunch and 14.4% at Nebius. Nebius’s six cards sit between 0% and 17.4% below its own on-demand rate, the six narrowest spot discounts of the 42 pairs on the site.

Its H100 SXM spot rate is worth one more comparison. The Cloud GPU Price Index closed the week of September 21, 2026 at $3.97 per GPU-hour, the median on-demand rate card across 18 providers. At $3.85 the spot rate is below that median, but not by much — and unlike an on-demand rate it can be interrupted, which is the whole of what the discount is meant to buy.

results.title: Analyst: AI Infrastructure Economics Hold – for Now
highlights:
That’s when far more computing capacity comes online and the industry must find enough demand for the resulting flood of AI tokens.

For now, money keeps flowing into the AI infrastructure machine even as costs rise. Bloomberg Intelligence estimated about six months ago that a leading-edge, 1-gigawatt AI data center built around Nvidia GB200 NVL72 systems would cost roughly $37.3 billion. Its latest bottom-up estimate puts the cost in the mid- to high-$40 billion range as prices increase for memory, storage, networking, electrical equipment, cooling and construction.

...

Many companies would be affected more by token costs, incurred from using AI models and tools, than the price of GPUs. This dynamic creates a potentially favorable equation as long as token output rises faster than chip costs.

...

It also creates the biggest risk. If each new generation of AI infrastructure can produce vastly more tokens, the industry eventually has to find buyers for them.

Kasibhotla described that as the critical unresolved question. Increasing the supply of AI output doesn’t guarantee that customers will continue paying the same price for it. Greater capacity could drive token prices down, particularly if demand fails to keep pace.

“As you push all these tokens into the market, will there be sufficient demand for it?” Kasibhotla asked. “Because if that doesn’t exist, then a lot of these other things will not exist. They will not be supported.”

For now, infrastructure builders are operating on the assumption that demand will absorb the additional capacity. Kasibhotla said companies also face competitive pressure to invest because they fear rivals could gain an advantage if they have access to more capable AI.

...

An example of how AI’s economics function is to look at the neoclouds, companies whose core business is to provide AI computing capacity by renting out chips, servers and related equipment. They are a pure play on the AI infrastructure business. 

“They are seeing inflation across the board,” Kasibhotla said. 

But they are able to pass along costs to clients. Bloomberg Intelligence found that CoreWeave raised prices about 25% across its offerings in July while contribution margins on recent contracts rose by 5 to 10 percentage points despite higher component costs. Nebius, meanwhile, has been able to charge $40 million to $50 million per megawatt for agreements shorter than six months, roughly twice its rates on one- to three-year contracts.

The useful life of GPUs is also turning out to be important.

Early neocloud contracts had long terms, customer prepayments and committed usage to help them finance their GPU purchases. Those arrangements could lock operators into prevailing prices even as costs rise. Moreover, IREN’s five-year Microsoft agreement, for example, assumed the GPUs would have no residual value when the contract ended, according to Bloomberg Intelligence.

It turns out that older hardware remains in demand. CoreWeave has contracted 2020-era Nvidia A100 GPUs through 2029, according to the report. That means older GPUs can continue generating revenue even after newer chips become available. Higher residual values reduce risk for lenders and can allow neoclouds to sign shorter customer agreements, giving them more opportunities to raise prices as costs increase.

results.title: CME GPU rental futures delayed by CFTC review to Nov 2026
highlights:
CME Group's plan to launch futures on Nvidia GPU rental prices by early October has stalled after the CFTC extended its review by 45 days to November 9, citing concerns about manipulation in the fragmented GPU rental market.

...

The CFTC's stated concern is the underlying market's structure itself: GPU rental pricing is fragmented across many neoclouds and hyperscalers with no centralized price discovery mechanism, the same problem that makes any new futures contract vulnerable to manipulation if reference prices aren't reliable.

CME had aimed for an early-October launch; the 45-day extension to November 9 means the contracts, if approved at all, arrive at the earliest in mid-November, delaying what would be a genuinely new way for AI infrastructure costs to be priced and hedged.

...

The delay itself is the story, not the eventual approval -- it confirms regulators think the GPU rental market is too fragmented to settle a futures contract against reliably, which is the same problem every AI infrastructure investor already deals with informally when comparing quotes across CoreWeave, Lambda and the hyperscalers. Until a reliable reference price exists, any 'compute cost' assumption in a startup's model is a negotiated number, not a market price -- diligence accordingly.

...

The CFTC's extended review is focused on the operational mechanics of the proposed contracts and is gathering broader industry input, driven by concern about potential market manipulation and the fragmented nature of the underlying GPU rental market. Unlike oil, wheat or even electricity, GPU rental pricing has no centralized exchange or standardized reference rate -- prices vary by chip generation, contract length, provider (CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe and the big three hyperscalers all price differently) and negotiating leverage between buyer and seller. A futures contract needs a reliable, hard-to-manipulate reference price to settle against, and regulators appear unconvinced that reference price currently exists in a market this fragmented.

results.title: Explainer: What are compute futures and how do they work? | FIA
highlights:
The cost of accessing that processing power has become significant enough that demand is emerging for something familiar to commodities markets: a derivatives market that allows buyers and sellers to manage the risk of future price changes.

...

A company does not necessarily have to own these chips. It can rent access to GPU capacity from cloud providers and specialist infrastructure companies. That makes it possible to put a price on the use of a particular type of processor, commonly expressed as the cost of renting one GPU for one hour. 

Not all GPU-hours are equal, however. The price can vary depending on the type and configuration of the GPU, its location, and the terms under which capacity is rented. That variability is one of the central challenges in creating a derivatives market for compute.

...

The basic idea is to create a futures contract whose value is tied to the cost of renting computing capacity. 

Contracts announced by CME Group and Silicon Data, a GPU market intelligence and benchmarking company, in August illustrate the model. 

CME plans to list futures based on Silicon Data's H100 and B200 Rental Indices, which measure the hourly rental cost of two models of Nvidia GPUs. Each contract represents 730 GPU-hours, roughly equivalent to one month of continuous capacity for a single GPU. At the time of writing, CME's planned launch on 5 October remains subject to regulatory review.

...

There is no single universal market price for compute. Prices vary across different GPUs, providers, locations and rental arrangements, so benchmark providers are trying to turn those disparate prices into representative reference rates. 

Silicon Data says its methodology collects GPU rental prices and makes adjustments designed to compare different rental arrangements on a more consistent basis. Ornn takes a transaction-based approach, with its Compute Price Index built from traded GPU compute prices. 

The aim is not to make every GPU rental identical. It is to create a trusted reference price against which a futures contract can settle.

results.title: 芝商所推出英伟达GPU租赁期货合约的计划遇阻，监管机构延长审查_新浪财经_新浪网
highlights:
据报道，旨在将英伟达GPU 租赁价格转化为可投资资产类别的相关期货合约的推出计划正遭遇阻碍。

 芝商所集团（CME Group）原计划最早于10月初推出这些合约，但届时将无法获得监管批准。一份致该交易所的信函显示，负责监管期货市场的美国商品期货交易委员会（CFTC）正在延长审查期限，以便深入研究此类合约的运作机制，并征求更广泛行业的意见。

 理论上，此类期货合约若辅以流动性充足的交易市场，将使人工智能公司和算力提供商能够提前锁定算力价格，从而对冲GPU租赁成本波动带来的风险。此外，对于在AI基础设施融资热潮中提供资金的贷款方而言，期货也能提供一种对冲手段，以规避作为抵押品的GPU发生贬值的风险。

 芝商所集团上月宣布，计划于10月5日推出算力期货，具体时间取决于监管部门的批准情况。该交易所将采用初创数据提供商Silicon Data的基准数据。其计划首批推出两款期货产品：一款基于英伟达（ Nvidia）H100芯片的租赁价格，另一款则基于英伟达B200芯片。

...

例如，GPU租赁价格通常是通过定制的私下合约确定的，而非通过大型公开市场形成。这就引发了一种可能性：市场主导者可能会操纵价格以谋取自身利益。当时，CFTC启动了为期60天的公众意见征询期，让市场参与者有机会就这些产品发表看法。

 此举曾让人怀疑芝商所能否按原定计划在10月份推出该产品，而CFTC在9月21日发出的信函中证实，该产品将不会在下个月如期上线。CFTC指出，鉴于该产品涉及“新颖或复杂”的问题，监管机构需要更多时间来评估芝商所的申请，因此决定将审查期延长45天，至11月9日。

results.title: Breakingviews - Bitcoin miners reveal the real AI scarcity trade | Reuters
highlights:
Follow
Show more companies
TORONTO, Sept 23 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Artificial intelligence requires two essential ingredients: electricity and silicon. Yet they are not equally valuable. During the cryptocurrency boom, companies snagged as much access to ​power as possible to fuel their bitcoin-mining facilities. With chatbots now ascendant, they are renting out this scarce ‌asset to AI operators. Those who choose to simply hawk electrons have won higher valuations than rivals hoarding electronics to offer full-service data centers. It’s a verdict on what the truly durable resource in a post-ChatGPT world will be.
Morgan Stanley analysts foresee 68 gigawatts of US data-center power demand between ​2026 and 2028, some 38 gigawatts more than projected supply. Crypto miners collectively control roughly 14 gigawatts of operational and ​planned capacity, Bernstein estimated in November.
